content.topic: DC Motor Back EMF and Speed Regulation
content.hook: Weaken the magnetic field of a DC motor, and it actually speeds up!
content.question: A DC shunt motor drives a constant torque load. If the field flux is halved while the terminal voltage is kept constant, what happens to the armature current?
explanation: In any DC machine, electromagnetic torque is directly proportional to both magnetic flux and armature current.
Because the mechanical load torque remains strictly constant, the product of flux and current must stay constant.
When you cut the field flux by half, the motor shaft momentarily decelerates due to torque deficit.
Back EMF is directly proportional to flux times speed, so back EMF drops instantly by half.
content.funFact: DC motors run dangerously fast if their field circuit opens accidentally, a condition called runaway.

script.narration: In any DC machine, electromagnetic torque is directly proportional to both magnetic flux and armature current.
Because the mechanical load torque remains strictly constant, the product of flux and current must stay constant.
When you cut the field flux by half, the motor shaft momentarily decelerates due to torque deficit.
Back EMF is directly proportional to flux times speed, so back EMF drops instantly by half.
With supply voltage fixed, the armature voltage drop equals supply voltage minus this lower back EMF value.
That sudden voltage imbalance forces the armature current to surge upwards until mechanical equilibrium is restored.
To produce the exact original torque with half the flux, the armature current must exactly double.
Speed then climbs higher until the newly established back EMF satisfies the steady armature current demand.
Therefore, under constant load torque, field flux weakening always forces armature current to increase inversely.
